source.title: Scaling Law Analysis in Federated Learning: How to Select the Optimal Model Size?
source.authors: Xuanyu Chen; Nan Yang; Shuai Wang; Dong Yuan

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses prior scaling-law work to motivate and assume an approximately convex relationship for selecting model size, but it does not test the claim versions' language-model loss laws or compute-versus-token/parameter allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on optimal model size in federated learning, including vision-model linear-probing accuracy and a model-size-versus-client-count trend. These do not measure the claim's held-out language-model cross-entropy power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Record the related federated-learning findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study relies on prior scaling-law work to assume a locally convex size–performance relation. It then derives and checks its own federated-learning result: optimal model size versus client count at fixed compute. It never measures held-out loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute for any model. Its vision experiments pick the optimal size by linear-probing accuracy over a sweep of only 10 sizes (11.6M–75.4M), which cannot show a loss power law or a compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. One correction: the empirical evidence is from vision models (ViT with MAE pretraining and linear probing; ResNet fine-tuning), not language models. The intro's mention of 'auto-regressive transformer' and 'final loss' does not match the experiments, which select the optimal size by accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fitting language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling curves, the study derives PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for federated SGD and uses linear-probing accuracy to select an optimal size in vision models. It compares centralized, federated, and single-client settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis and results vary with the number of clients and data partitioning; the default non-IID partition uses Dirichlet α = 0.1. CIFAR-100 and ImageNet are evaluated separately.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed total compute, the optimal ViT size (by linear-probing accuracy) falls with client count. Fitted log-log slopes are in [−0.28, −0.48], with R² > 0.88.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In federated training at fixed total compute, optimal model size decreases roughly as a negative power of the number of clients.

fits_no_version.finding: With equal total data and compute, federated models have lower linear-probing accuracy than centralized ones, and the gap widens with more clients.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data decentralization lowers the best achievable generalization at equal compute.

fits_no_version.finding: The federated optimal size is close to the average of the single-client optima, for both ViT and ResNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The federated optimal model size is set by average per-client compute.

record.problems: The empirical evidence uses vision models and linear-probing accuracy rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. The text does not give numerical per-model or per-client results for the figures, and it reports no uncertainty estimates. The theoretical conclusions depend on multiple stated assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows were left out.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no loss curves are reported.
Extrapolating fitted laws to much larger runs.
How loss-minimising parameter and token counts grow with compute; compute is held fixed and only client count varies.
Shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Vision models are trained, but no power law of loss or accuracy in size, data or compute is fitted.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss; linear-probing accuracy is used only to select the best size.
Dependence of exponents or the compute-optimal split on fitting or setup choices.

record.verdict_notes: There are internal inconsistencies. The intro describes an auto-regressive transformer and loss analysis, but the experiments use ViT/MAE and accuracy. Appendix Table 1 lists IID client data and up to 50 clients, while the main text gives Dirichlet α=0.1 non-IID partitions and figures with up to 150 clients. There are no uncertainty estimates, and the size sweep spans less than one order of magnitude.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
How loss-minimising parameter and token counts vary with compute budget.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same loss power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes; the paper studies vision models but does not measure that loss relationship.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of the claimed loss-law exponents and compute-optimal split on fitting choices or setup.
